brief:
Lebanese authorities arrested Ashraf Dabbour, the Palestinian Authority's former ambassador in Beirut, at the city's airport on Monday — at Ramallah's request and ahead of extradition on embezzlement charges, a Lebanese judicial official told AFP. Four months earlier, Dabbour had publicly accused the man now at the centre of two Palestinian power struggles at once: Yasser Abbas, the president's son.

The arrest closes one act of a fight that has run all year. This report lays out what the published record establishes about that fight, and about a second collision — over the West Bank's fuel — that Palestinians are connecting to the same name; and it is precise about what the record does not yet establish.

## The envoy's file

Dabbour served as ambassador in Beirut from 2012 until 2025, when President Mahmoud Abbas dismissed him. The dismissal followed the president's decision to send his son Yasser to Lebanon to oversee the sale of land and properties belonging to the Palestine Liberation Organization there — a mandate reported at the time by Asharq Al-Awsat and the wire agencies, and one that put the son and the sitting ambassador on the same ground.

In April, on his own Facebook page, the dismissed envoy named his adversary:

> He is exploiting his control over the security services and his influence within the Authority to settle his personal scores — pursuing me with arrest warrants from one place to another.
> Ashraf Dabbour on Yasser Abbas, Facebook, April 2026

The Authority's answer is the case file: prosecutors charge Dabbour with corruption and embezzlement of funds during his tenure, and it was a Palestinian warrant that Lebanese judges acted on when he landed on Monday, L'Orient Today reported from Beirut. Dabbour denies the charges and says they are designed to tarnish his reputation. No trial has yet tested either account — the extradition will.

## The fuel file

The second collision is unfolding at the West Bank's petrol pumps. Palestinian security services raided fuel stations belonging to the businessman Tareq al-Natsheh in several cities and detained him, Ultra Palestine reported — the owner of the Al-Huda chain, whose 22 stations joined July's coordinated strike over the banking crisis that the Associated Press documented. Within days of his detention, the Palestinian Press Network reported, petrol and diesel were running out across Ramallah governorate's stations.

Behind the detention sits a documented debt: the Authority owes fuel suppliers mounting arrears, part of the same fiscal breakdown this newspaper mapped in its budget reporting. What sits beside it is so far only reported, not established: Palestinian outlets, the Palestinian Press Network among them, carry accounts that the Authority is preparing a new company to centralise fuel purchasing — to be headed, those accounts say, by Yasser Abbas. No official body has confirmed the company, named its ownership, or explained the detention. Al-Natsheh, whom the same outlets describe as close to Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh, has not been charged publicly.

## What is established, and what is not

The record establishes this much. Yasser Abbas entered Fatah's Central Committee in May, eighth of eighteen, as [our congress deep dive](https://www.timesofpalestine.com/en/story/4fb4204cb0.html) reported. He holds his father's mandate over PLO property sales in Lebanon. The former ambassador who publicly accused him of turning the security services on a critic is now in a Beirut cell awaiting transfer. The fuel magnate whose sector the Authority owes money is in a Palestinian one. Those are facts with documents and dates behind them.

What no published document establishes is the connecting line: that the son directs these cases, that the cases serve his interests, or that the two files are one file. No court has joined them; no official has answered the accusation Dabbour posted in April, and none has commented on the fuel company reports at all.

In a system with working oversight, that silence would end in a hearing. The Palestinian Authority has had no sitting parliament since 2007, and [every security service involved answers to presidential decree alone](https://www.timesofpalestine.com/en/story/906aa59f99.html). When the activist Suhaib Zahda sought a permit in Hebron to protest fuel prices and corruption, the Preventive Security Service arrested him too, The Jerusalem Post reported this week.

So the questions Palestinians are asking about the president's son are being asked in Facebook posts and at empty petrol pumps, because no institution exists to ask them anywhere else. That — whatever the extradition eventually proves or disproves — is the condition this newspaper can already report.
